example_01.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_01.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, delete, and watch permissions on pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any user with valid credentials can manage all pods in the webapp namespace. This is a security risk because it allows authenticated users to perform actions that could disrupt or compromise the web application.

example_02.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants read-only access to a broad set of resources across the entire cluster. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated users — meaning any user who has authenticated with the cluster. This is appropriate for monitoring purposes as it allows legitimate users to view the status of various resources without granting them write permissions or access to sensitive data.

example_03.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_03.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on deployments as well as get, list, create, and update permissions on services. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate, create, update, and delete deployments and services in the cicd namespace. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_04.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_04.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the database namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any user with valid credentials can enumerate all secrets in the database namespace. This is a misconfiguration because it allows any authenticated user to access sensitive information that should be restricted to specific users or service accounts.

example_05.category: Overly broad cluster-wide RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_05.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on nodes, node statuses, node metrics, and persistent volumes. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate all nodes, their statuses, metrics, and persistent volumes across the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_06.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_06.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on configmaps in the logging namespace. It also grants get, list, and watch permissions on pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can perform these actions. This is a misconfiguration because it allows any authenticated user to modify critical configuration data and enumerate all pods in the logging namespace.

example_07.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to authenticated users
example_07.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on service accounts across the entire cluster. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can create or modify service accounts in any namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_08.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to unauthenticated users
example_08.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, watch permissions on pods and create permission on pod exec resources. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate all pods in the development namespace and execute commands inside them. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_09.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_09.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on ingresses as well as get, list, and watch permissions on services and endpoints. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage ingress resources and view service and endpoint details in the ingress-nginx namespace. This is a misconfiguration because it grants overly broad permissions to all authenticated users, which could potentially allow unauthorized access or modifications to critical routing configurations.

example_10.category: Overly broad cluster-wide RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_10.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants full administrative access within tenant namespaces for self-service provisioning. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can perform all actions on a wide range of resources across the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_11.category: Overly broad permissions for static web server
example_11.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a webapp-nginx workload running nginx:1.25 and explicitly states in its annotation that it serves static HTTP content. However, the role.yaml grants create, update, patch, delete permissions on pods, deployments, and services in the webapp namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all three files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for these permissions, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_12.category: Overly broad permissions for a cache service
example_12.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a redis-cache workload running Redis. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create, and delete permissions on pods; get, list, update, and patch permissions on deployments; and get, list, create, update, and patch permissions on configmaps in the caching namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the redis-cache-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. A cache service like Redis typically does not need such broad permissions — it should not be creating or deleting pods, updating deployments, or modifying configmaps. This misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together.

example_13.category: Unnecessary delete permissions on critical resources
example_13.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a prometheus-scraper workload running Prometheus. The role.yaml grants get, list, watch, create and delete permissions on pods, deployments, services, and endpoints in the monitoring namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the prometheus-scraper-sa ServiceAccount which is used by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all three files together — the workload does not need delete access to these resources for its stated purpose of collecting metrics.

example_14.category: Overly broad permissions for a static file server
example_14.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a static-fileserver workload running nginx:1.25 and explicitly states in its annotation that it serves uploaded assets over HTTP. However, the role.yaml grants full CRUD permissions on services, ingresses, and endpoints in the fileserver namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the fileserver-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all three files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for such broad permissions, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_15.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a postgres-db workload running PostgreSQL. The role.yaml grants excessive permissions including create, update, patch, and delete on deployments; get, list, watch, and delete on pods; create on pod exec; and get, list, create, and delete on persistentvolumeclaims. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the postgres-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. A database workload does not need these permissions — it only needs read access to its own pods and PVCs, and should not be able to modify or delete them.

example_16.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a frontend-react workload running node:20-alpine and serving a React single-page application. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, and delete permissions on services and endpoints, as well as get, list, update, and patch permissions on deployments in the frontend namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the frontend-react-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. A React single-page application typically does not need such broad permissions over service resources — especially create, update, delete, and patch permissions.

example_17.category: Excessive permissions on pods and deployments
example_17.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an nginx-proxy workload. The role.yaml grants the nginx-proxy-role excessive permissions, including create, update, patch, delete on deployments and create, delete on pods within the proxy namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the nginx-proxy-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the nginx-proxy deployment. A reverse proxy workload does not typically need such broad permissions over other pods and deployments in its own namespace.

example_18.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Elasticsearch cluster for storing and indexing application logs. The role.yaml grants extensive permissions, including create, update, patch, delete on persistentvolumeclaims, deployments, statefulsets, and pods within the logging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the elasticsearch-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the Elasticsearch deployment. This configuration allows the Elasticsearch workload to perform critical operations such as deleting pods and managing storage resources, which could be exploited if the service account or the Elasticsearch instance itself were compromised.

example_19.category: Overly broad permissions on core resources
example_19.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a RabbitMQ message broker. The role.yaml grants the rabbitmq-role very broad permissions: it can get, list, watch, create, and delete pods; get, list, create, update, and delete services; and get, list, update, and patch deployments — all within the messaging namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this overly permissive role to the rabbitmq-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the RabbitMQ deployment. A message broker does not typically need such extensive permissions on core Kubernetes resources. This misconfiguration only becomes apparent when reading all three files together.

example_20.category: Overly broad permissions for a metrics exporter
example_20.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an nginx-exporter workload running nginx/nginx-prometheus-exporter:0.11 and explicitly states in its annotation that it exposes basic HTTP metrics endpoint. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, watch, update, patch, and delete permissions on deployments; get, list, watch, and delete permissions on pods; and get, list, create, and delete permissions on services. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the nginx-exporter-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for such broad permissions, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_21.category: NetworkPolicy misconfiguration due to label mismatch
example_21.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a frontend workload with the label app: frontend. The networkpolicy.yaml specifies an ingress policy that only allows traffic from pods with the label role: ingress-controller, but it selects pods with the label app: web-frontend. This mismatch means the NetworkPolicy does not actually protect the frontend pods as intended, because the podSelector in the NetworkPolicy does not match any pods defined by the Deployment. The misconfiguration is only visible when both files are read together.

example_22.category: Overly permissive network policy for database pods
example_22.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a postgres workload with the label app: postgres. The networkpolicy.yaml isolates postgres pods from unauthorised ingress traffic, but it only selects pods with the label tier: database. Since the postgres pod does not have this label, it will not be selected by the NetworkPolicy and thus will not benefit from the isolation rules defined. This misconfiguration is only visible when reading both files together — the deployment file shows the actual labels used by the postgres pod, while the network policy file shows the labels it selects on.

example_23.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Prometheus workload with the label app: prometheus. The network policy yaml specifies a NetworkPolicy that restricts ingress to pods with the label app: Prometheus (note the capital 'P'). This mismatch in labeling means the NetworkPolicy will not apply to the Prometheus pod, allowing unrestricted ingress traffic. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes the correct label for the Prometheus pod, while the network policy incorrectly capitalizes the label, failing to protect the pod as intended.

example_24.category: Overly permissive network policy for payment API pods
example_24.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a payment-api workload with the label app: payment-api. The networkpolicy.yaml restricts ingress to these pods but allows egress traffic to any pod with the label app: postgres, regardless of namespace or environment. This means that the payment API pods can communicate with any PostgreSQL database in the cluster, potentially exposing sensitive transaction data to unauthorized databases. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the deployment establishes the workload handles sensitive transactions, while the network policy allows unrestricted egress to all postgres pods.

example_25.category: Network policy misconfiguration due to label mismatch
example_25.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Elasticsearch cluster with pods labeled app=elasticsearch. The networkpolicy.yaml aims to isolate these Elasticsearch pods but uses a podSelector that matches pods with the label app=elastic, which does not match any pods defined in the provided files. This misconfiguration means the NetworkPolicy will not apply to the Elasticsearch pods as intended, leaving them potentially exposed to unauthorized ingress traffic.

example_26.category: Network policy misconfiguration due to label mismatch
example_26.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a RabbitMQ message broker with the label role: rabbitmq. The networkpolicy.yaml specifies a NetworkPolicy named rabbitmq-isolation-policy that isolates pods with the label role: message-broker, allowing ingress and egress only from/to pods with the label app: worker. However, the labels do not match — the deployment uses role: rabbitmq while the network policy expects role: message-broker. This misconfiguration means the NetworkPolicy will not apply to the RabbitMQ pods, leaving them unprotected and potentially exposed to unauthorized traffic.

example_27.category: NetworkPolicy misconfiguration due to incorrect pod selector
example_27.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Jenkins CI/CD controller with the label app: jenkins. The networkpolicy.yaml is intended to restrict ingress to Jenkins pods but uses an incorrect podSelector matchLabels role: build-agent, which does not match any labels defined in the provided files. This misconfiguration means the NetworkPolicy will not apply to the Jenkins deployment, leaving it exposed to unauthorized ingress traffic.

example_28.category: NetworkPolicy misconfiguration due to label mismatch
example_28.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Deployment named react-app with the label app: react-app. The networkpolicy.yaml defines a NetworkPolicy that selects pods based on the label app: reactapp, which does not match the label used in the deployment. This mismatch means the NetworkPolicy will not apply to the intended pods, potentially allowing unauthorized ingress traffic to the React application pods.

example_29.category: Network policy misconfiguration with incorrect pod selector
example_29.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an api-gateway workload with the label app: api-gateway. The networkpolicy.yaml specifies a NetworkPolicy named api-gateway-policy that is intended to restrict ingress and egress for the API gateway pods. However, the podSelector in the NetworkPolicy uses role: api-gateway instead of app: api-gateway. This misconfiguration means the NetworkPolicy will not apply to the api-gateway pods defined in the deployment.yaml, leaving them unprotected by the intended network restrictions.

example_30.justification: The network policy worker-isolation-policy is intended to isolate the job-processor pods, but it does not select the worker pods defined in deployment.yaml. The podSelector in the NetworkPolicy specifies role: job-processor, while the Deployment labels its pods with role: worker. As a result, the NetworkPolicy does not apply to the worker pods, leaving them unprotected by the intended isolation policy.

example_31.category: Overly permissive ClusterRoleBinding to CI/CD pipeline service account
example_31.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named cicd-pipeline-manager that grants permissions to bind cluster roles and manage deployments. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the cicd-deploy-sa ServiceAccount in the cicd namespace. This configuration is problematic because it grants the CI/CD pipeline service account broad permissions, including the ability to bind any cluster role to any subject. This level of access is typically reserved for administrative tasks and poses a significant security risk if compromised.

example_32.category: Unrestricted role escalation for Prometheus service account
example_32.justification: The role.yaml grants the escalate verb on roles, which allows a subject to modify its own permissions. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the prometheus-sa ServiceAccount. This means that if an attacker compromises the Prometheus service account, they can escalate their privileges within the monitoring namespace by modifying the roles assigned to it.

example_33.category: Cluster admin privileges granted to a user
example_33.justification: The target_clusterrolebinding.yaml grants cluster-admin privileges to the platform-admin user. This is a highly privileged role that allows full administrative access to the entire Kubernetes cluster, including the ability to create and delete resources, modify configurations, and access sensitive data. Granting such broad permissions to any single user poses significant security risks.

example_34.category: Overly broad RBAC permissions for deployment automation user
example_34.justification: The role.yaml grants the devops-role-binder Role get, list, and bind permissions on roles within the rbac.authorization.k8s.io API group. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the devops-automation-user User. This means that the user has the ability to create new RoleBindings for any other subject in the cluster, which could potentially grant them excessive privileges. Additionally, the same Role grants get, list, watch permissions on deployments within the apps API group. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_35.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named security-audit-escalator that includes the escalate verb on clusterroles resources. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the security-team group. The escalate verb is not a standard Kubernetes RBAC verb and its presence in a ClusterRole suggests a potential for unintended privilege escalation. This misconfiguration becomes apparent only when both files are read together, as the ClusterRole alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_36.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants the ability to impersonate any service account and create tokens for them. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this role to the workflow-engine-sa ServiceAccount in the platform namespace, meaning it can impersonate any service account in the cluster. Additionally, the target_serviceaccount.yaml defines a high-privilege service account (cluster-provisioner-sa) with full administrative access to the cluster. The misconfiguration is only visible by reading all three files together: the ClusterRole grants broad impersonation permissions, and the ClusterRoleBinding binds this role to a specific ServiceAccount, which can then be used to impersonate any other service account in the cluster, including high-privilege ones.

example_37.category: Overly permissive cluster role binding to service account
example_37.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines a ClusterRole named platform-rbac-manager that allows managing RBAC bindings and escalating roles. The target_clusterrole.yaml defines another ClusterRole named platform-admin which grants full administrative access to all resources and non-resource URLs. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds the platform-rbac-manager role to the platform-automation-sa ServiceAccount, allowing it to bind any other role, including the platform-admin role, to itself or other subjects. This creates a security risk because the platform-automation-sa ServiceAccount can escalate its own privileges to full administrative access, which is only visible by reading all three files together.

example_38.category: Unrestricted group impersonation leading to full cluster access
example_38.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants the ability to impersonate any group and get, list users. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the infra-automation-user User. This means that the infra-automation-user can impersonate any group in the cluster, including system:masters. Since system:masters is bound to cluster-admin by default, this effectively grants full cluster access to the infra-automation-user.

example_39.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to a group of users
example_39.justification: The role.yaml defines a ClusterRole named platform-clusterrole-binder that grants permissions to get, list, and bind cluster roles, as well as get, list, and watch service accounts across the entire cluster. The rolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the group platform-engineers. This configuration allows any member of the platform-engineers group to bind any cluster role to any subject, including other users or service accounts, effectively granting them broad administrative privileges over the entire cluster.

example_40.category: Overly permissive ClusterRole with impersonation permissions bound to a ServiceAccount
example_40.justification: The clusterrole.yaml defines the tenant-admin-manager ClusterRole, which grants escalate and impersonate permissions on serviceaccounts and users. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to the tenant-provisioner-sa ServiceAccount in the tenants namespace. This configuration allows the tenant provisioning service account to impersonate any user or serviceaccount, and escalate privileges within the cluster. This is a significant security risk because it grants excessive permissions that could be exploited for unauthorized access.

example_41.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_41.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a webapp-nginx workload running nginx:1.25 and explicitly states in its annotation that it serves pre-built static HTML files with no backend or credentials required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the webapp namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the webapp-nginx-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_43.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a blackbox-exporter workload running prom/blackbox-exporter:0.24.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it probes unauthenticated public HTTP and ICMP endpoints only, with no configSecret or credential volume mounts used, and no authentication credentials required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the probing namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the blackbox-exporter-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. example_44.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Memcached in-memory key-value cache workload and explicitly states in its annotation that it requires no Kubernetes secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the caching namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the memcached-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_45.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a statsd-exporter workload running prom/statsd-exporter:v0.26.0 and explicitly states in its annotation that it receives StatsD metrics over UDP and exposes them as Prometheus metrics, with no credentials or secrets required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the metrics namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the prometheus-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_46.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_46.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a caddy-frontend workload running caddy:2.7 and explicitly states in its annotation that it serves pre-built React static assets over HTTP on port 80 only, with no TLS configuration, no backend integration, and no credentials required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the frontend namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the caddy-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_47.category: Unnecessary secret access for metrics exporter
example_47.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a graphite-exporter workload running prom/graphite-exporter:0.13.3 and explicitly states in its annotation that it receives Graphite metrics over TCP and exposes them as Prometheus metrics, with no credentials or secrets required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the redis namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the redis-exporter-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_48.category: Unnecessary secret access for public service endpoint healthcheck
example_48.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a curl-based HTTP healthcheck probe workload that explicitly states in its annotation it polls only public service endpoints and requires no credentials or secrets. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the staging namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the healthcheck-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the deployment establishes the workload has no legitimate need for secret access, while the role and binding establish it has been granted exactly that.

example_49.category: Unnecessary secret access for static web server
example_49.justification: The deployment.yaml defines an Apache httpd workload serving static documentation content over HTTP only, with no dynamic backend or TLS configuration. The annotation explicitly states that no credentials are required. However, the role.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets in the docs namespace, and the rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the httpd-sa ServiceAccount, which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. example_50.category: Unnecessary secret access for diagnostic service
example_50.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a whoami diagnostic service running traefik/whoami:v1.10 and explicitly states in its annotation that it returns HTTP request metadata only, with no credentials or secrets required. example_76.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_76.justification: The role.yaml grants get, list, create, delete, and watch permissions on persistentvolumeclaims. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage all PersistentVolumeClaims in the storage namespace. This is a security misconfiguration because it allows any authenticated user to perform critical operations on PVCs, which could lead to data loss or unauthorized access to storage resources.

example_77.category: Cluster-wide secret access to unauthenticated users
example_77.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants get, list, and watch permissions on all secrets across the entire cluster. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:unauthenticated, meaning any unauthenticated user — with no credentials at all — can enumerate all secrets in every namespace of the cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_78.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_78.justification: The role.yaml grants full management permissions on NetworkPolicy resources in the api namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any user with valid credentials can manage network policies for the entire api namespace. This is a security risk because it allows any authenticated user to modify network policies, potentially disrupting or exposing the API services.

example_79.category: Overly broad cluster role binding to authenticated users
example_79.justification: The clusterrole.yaml grants bind permissions on ClusterRoles and get, list, create, update permissions on ClusterRoleBindings. The clusterrolebinding.yaml binds this ClusterRole to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can manage all ClusterRoles and ClusterRoleBindings in the entire cluster. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together — the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_80.category: Overly broad RBAC binding to authenticated users
example_80.justification: The role.yaml grants create permissions on serviceaccount/token resources and get, list permissions on serviceaccounts. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to system:authenticated, meaning any authenticated user can create tokens for any ServiceAccount in the staging namespace. This misconfiguration is only visible by reading both files together: the role file alone does not reveal the dangerous subject, and the binding file alone does not reveal the sensitive permissions being granted.

example_81.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Grafana dashboard service. The role.yaml grants permissions to manage configmaps and services within the monitoring namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the grafana-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the Grafana deployment. The serviceaccount.yaml defines the grafana-sa ServiceAccount. Reading all files together confirms that the permissions granted are appropriate for a dashboard service managing its own configmaps and services within its namespace.

example_82.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a Jenkins CI server workload. The role.yaml grants permissions to manage pods and service accounts, as well as read-only access to deployments within the cicd namespace. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the jenkins-sa ServiceAccount, which is used by the Jenkins deployment. The serviceaccount.yaml defines the jenkins-sa ServiceAccount. Reading all files together confirms that the permissions granted are appropriate for a CI server workload — it legitimately needs to manage pods and service accounts, and read deployment status within its own namespace.

example_83.category: Overly broad secret access and pod exec permissions
example_83.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a memcached workload. The role.yaml grants get, list, create, update, patch, delete permissions on all secrets in the caching namespace and create permissions on pods/exec as well as get, list, watch permissions on pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this Role to the memcached-sa ServiceAccount which is the same ServiceAccount mounted by the deployment. The misconfiguration only becomes visible by reading all four files together — the workload does not require such broad secret access or pod exec permissions.

example_84.category: Unnecessary permissions on deployments and pods
example_84.justification: The deployment.yaml defines a MongoDB workload. The role.yaml grants the mongodb-role get, list, watch, delete permissions on deployments in the database namespace as well as get, list, and watch permissions on pods. The rolebinding.yaml binds this role to the mongodb-sa ServiceAccount which is used by the MongoDB deployment. example_85.category: Overly broad permissions for a tracing system

A tracing system typically does not need such broad permissions — it should only require read access to relevant resources for monitoring purposes. The misconfiguration becomes apparent when reading all four files together: the deployment establishes the workload as a tracing system, while the role and binding establish it has been granted unnecessary administrative permissions.

example_86.category: Network policy misconfiguration due to missing environment label on Solr pods
example_86.justification: The networkpolicy.yaml defines a NetworkPolicy that restricts ingress to Solr pods based on the environment label.
